description: A class of novel synthetic compounds that act as ecdysone receptor agonists. In this text they are described as attractive candidates for pest control, research tools, gene therapy applications, and inducing transgenic gene expression in plants, with selective insecticidal activity and relative safety for mammals.

A chemical subclass of nonsteroidal ecdysone agonists highlighted as potent members of the class. They are the specific compounds developed as insecticides and discussed for their biological activity and selectivity.
A diacylhydrazine-derived nonsteroidal ecdysone agonist developed as an insecticide. It is one of the four named compounds in the review and is noted for strong activity against Lepidoptera.
A diacylhydrazine-derived nonsteroidal ecdysone agonist developed as an insecticide. It is one of the four named compounds and is described as effective against Lepidoptera.
A diacylhydrazine-derived nonsteroidal ecdysone agonist developed as an insecticide. It is one of the four named compounds and is described as effective against Lepidoptera.

A diacylhydrazine-derived nonsteroidal ecdysone agonist developed as an insecticide. It is one of the four named compounds and is described as effective against Coleoptera and only mildly active against Lepidoptera.
The transcriptional process regulated by ecdysone agonists in this context. The compounds function as ligands for gene expression and are used to induce transgenic gene expression in plants.

A therapeutic application area in which nonsteroidal ecdysone agonists are used as molecular tools to control gene expression. In the text, it is presented as a downstream application of their ligand activity.
Induced expression of introduced genes in plant systems. The text states that nonsteroidal ecdysone agonists have been applied to induce this process.

An applied agricultural use category for the compounds described in the review. Nonsteroidal ecdysone agonists are presented as attractive candidates for this role because of their narrow spectrum of activity.
A pesticide application category for the named diacylhydrazines. The compounds were developed as insecticides and are described as toxic to insects but safe for mammals.
A broader agricultural chemical category that includes the nonsteroidal ecdysone agonists discussed here. Their narrow spectrum of activity is said to make them relatively safe as pesticides.
An insect order used here as the target pest population for several of the compounds. The first three named compounds are effective against this group.
An insect order used as a comparative target population in the selectivity profile of the compounds. The first three named compounds are weakly active or inactive against this group.

An insect order used as a comparative target population in the selectivity profile of the compounds. Halofenozide is effective against this group, while the first three compounds are weakly active or inactive.
A non-target vertebrate population mentioned as being safe from toxicity of these compounds. Their safety for mammals is emphasized as part of the favorable selectivity profile.
The plant host system in which transgenic gene expression can be induced by nonsteroidal ecdysone agonists. They are relevant as a biological application context rather than a target pest.

The molecular mode of action described for nonsteroidal ecdysone agonists. They function as ligands that regulate gene expression, providing the mechanistic basis for their research and therapeutic applications.

A steroid hormone that functions as the central regulatory agent in insect developmental transitions. In this text, it controls molting and metamorphosis, acts through nuclear hormone receptors, and drives transcriptional programs required for cell death and tissue deletion.

Receptor proteins that mediate ecdysone signaling by linking the hormone to spatial and temporal regulation of gene transcription. They are the molecular interface through which ecdysone influences developmental and cell-death-related gene expression.

The process of producing RNA from genes, here regulated by ecdysone signaling. It includes transcription of genes required for cell death and is a key downstream mechanism in developmental tissue remodeling.

Programmed elimination of cells, described here as a gene-regulated process required for developmental tissue removal. It is a downstream biological outcome of ecdysone-controlled transcriptional programs.
A developmental transition in insects regulated by ecdysone. It represents one of the essential hormone-controlled processes associated with metamorphic progression.
The insect developmental transformation regulated by ecdysone. It provides the broader biological context in which tissue deletion and larval tissue remodeling occur.
The developmental removal of larval tissues that are no longer needed during metamorphosis. This process is orchestrated by pulses of ecdysone and is central to tissue remodeling.
A larval tissue specifically identified as being deleted during insect metamorphosis. It serves as a tissue target of ecdysone-dependent developmental cell death.
A larval tissue identified as one of the obsolete tissues removed during metamorphosis. It is a target of ecdysone-dependent tissue deletion in insects.
A model insect genus used in studies of ecdysone-dependent cell and tissue removal. It is highlighted as a key experimental system for understanding the molecular machinery and mechanisms involved.
An insect group used as a comparative model for studying ecdysone-dependent developmental tissue deletion. They provide biological context for conserved mechanisms of metamorphic remodeling.

Temporal bursts of the steroid hormone ecdysone that act as the signaling scenario driving metamorphic tissue deletion. The timing and periodicity of these pulses are important for orchestrating developmental transitions.

A broad invertebrate animal group used here as comparative biological models for studying molecular function, endocrinology, and genetics. The text frames arthropods as the ancestral lineage from which insects descended and as a domain-relevant population for evolutionary and developmental research.

Representative insect experimental models used to investigate endocrinology and genetics. They serve as established comparative systems in the text and are contrasted with non-insect arthropods for their historical role in shaping current understanding.

A canonical insect model organism referenced as the benchmark beyond which other representative insect models have been adopted. It functions as a key comparative model in molecular and developmental biology.
Arthropod taxa outside the insect lineage that are highlighted as underexplored models with potential to provide new insight into endocrinology, genetics, and developmental biology.

A major arthropod group described as ancient and diverse, comprising many life histories and ecological roles. In the text, crustaceans are the focal subject for understanding metamorphosis and endocrine regulation.
A developmental transformation process in crustaceans described as ubiquitous, challenging, and highly studied. It is the central biological process whose endocrine control is being reviewed.
The study of hormonal regulation and endocrine mechanisms, here specifically the biological framework underlying crustacean metamorphosis and comparative arthropod development.

A conserved endocrine signaling cascade centered on ecdysone that is emphasized as the focus of the review. It is presented as a key regulatory system for crustacean metamorphosis and a target for future molecular investigation.
A steroid hormone central to the ecdysone cascade and endocrine control of arthropod development. It functions as the molecular driver of the signaling system discussed in relation to metamorphosis.

High-throughput molecular profiling approaches used to enable exploratory molecular research. In the text, these technologies are expected to uncover crustacean-specific components and pathways involved in metamorphosis.
Exploratory investigation of molecular components and pathways, enabled by omics technologies. It is described as the research mode that may reveal crustacean-specific biology.

entity_name: COMPONENTS AND PATHWAYS UNIQUE TO CRUSTACEANS
description: Crustacean-specific molecular components and signaling pathways hypothesized to exist beyond well-studied insect systems. These are the putative mechanistic elements sought through comparative and omics-based research.

An evolutionary outcome reflecting the ability of arthropods to adapt across time. The text states that understanding the ecdysone system and crustacean metamorphosis provides deeper insight into this broader endpoint.

The insect model organism discussed in the review. It serves as the experimental system in which inter-organ communication, neuroendocrine control, and steroid hormone signaling are studied to understand metamorphosis.

The immature developmental stage that must grow to sufficient size before maturation begins. It is the population stratum whose developmental timing is regulated by endocrine and inter-organ signaling.

A major developmental transition in insects that is controlled by steroid hormones and triggered by ecdysone. It is the central biological process discussed in relation to growth, maturation, and inter-organ signaling.
A major developmental transition in mammals mentioned as an analogous steroid-hormone-controlled process. It provides comparative context for developmental timing and maturation control.
Endocrine signaling molecules that control major developmental transitions, including metamorphosis in insects and puberty in mammals. They function as upstream regulators of developmental timing.
The steroid hormone produced under neuroendocrine control that triggers metamorphosis in insects. It is a key molecular signal linking inter-organ communication to developmental transition.

The integrated signaling system that coordinates hormonal control of development by assessing nutrient availability and organ growth status. It mediates inter-organ communication and regulates ecdysone production.

Signals exchanged between different organs that mediate crosstalk and inform the neuroendocrine system about growth status and nutrient availability. They are central to coordinating maturation timing.
A physiological state sensed by the neuroendocrine system to determine whether maturation should proceed. It acts as an input to developmental timing control.
The developmental and size state of internal organs, which is assessed by the neuroendocrine system to ensure maturation occurs at the appropriate time.
The developmental progression toward adult form and reproductive fitness. It is coordinated with growth and initiated only when sufficient size and internal organ status are achieved.
The increase in organismal or organ size that must be coordinated with maturation. It is part of the developmental balance controlled by inter-organ signaling.
The network of signaling interactions among organs that controls the timing of metamorphosis. These networks define principles of growth and maturation coordination.
Major life-stage changes such as metamorphosis and puberty that are regulated by steroid hormones. This is a broader developmental process category referenced in the text.
The insect model organism discussed in the review, used to study how steroid hormone signaling times developmental progression and stage-specific gene regulation.

The moulting steroid hormone that acts as the key developmental signal in insects, driving timed transitions such as larval moults, pupation, and metamorphosis and regulating tissue-specific growth and cell identity.
The hormone-driven signaling process mediated by ecdysone that produces temporal and tissue-specific transcriptional responses during insect development.

The receptor complex formed by Ecdysone Receptor and Ultraspiracle that mediates ecdysone-dependent transcriptional regulation, repressing target genes in the absence of hormone and enabling activation when hormone levels rise.
A receptor component of the ecdysone receptor heterodimer that participates in hormone-dependent gene regulation in Drosophila development.
A receptor component that partners with Ecdysone Receptor to form the ecdysone receptor heterodimer and regulate primary response gene expression.
Early hormone-responsive genes whose expression is repressed by the ecdysone receptor heterodimer in the absence of ecdysone and de-repressed as hormone titre rises.
The ordered progression through insect developmental stages that depends on precisely timed ecdysone pulses.
Developmental molting events in larvae that are guided by timed ecdysone pulses.
The developmental transition to the pupal stage, described as one of the milestones controlled by ecdysone timing.
The major developmental reorganization process in insects that is coordinated by ecdysone signaling.
The acquisition of cell identities and tissue organization that is coordinated by ecdysone in a tissue-specific manner.
Tissue-specific growth regulated by ecdysone signaling during insect development.
The regulatory control of transcriptional responses underlying stage-appropriate ecdysone signaling specificity.
The temporally restricted transcriptional and developmental responses to ecdysone that occur at the correct developmental stage.
The contextual framework in which ecdysone signaling elicits distinct repressive and activating responses depending on developmental time and tissue type.
The circulating hormone level or concentration of ecdysone, which rises to relieve repression of target primary response genes.

The broad insect population discussed in the paper as the biological subject of lipid transport and storage physiology. The text emphasizes that lipid dependence varies with developmental stage and across species, making this the central population context for the described transport mechanisms.

A life-history stratum of insects that influences the extent to which lipid metabolism supports metabolic needs. It functions as a modifying population context for the lipid transport and storage patterns described in the abstract.

The primary storage organ in insects and a major metabolic center. It stores neutral lipids as triglycerides and serves as the source tissue from which diglycerides and sterols are mobilized into the hemolymph.

The circulating internal fluid bathing insect tissues and organs. It functions as the transport medium for nutrient substrates, metabolic wastes, lipids, sterols, and hormones, and contains specific lipoprotein classes involved in these transport processes.
Neutral lipid storage form in insects, accumulated in the fat body and mobilized during times of need. They represent the stored precursor pool for lipid transport into the hemolymph.

A neutral lipid transport form released from the fat body into the hemolymph in many insects. They constitute a major hemolymph lipid fraction and are carried by specific lipoproteins for distribution to utilization sites.
A sterol transported from the gut into the hemolymph by lipoprotein I. It is part of the insect lipid transport system described as being regulated by specific hemolymph lipoproteins.

A class of hemolymph-associated lipid carriers that bind diglycerides and enable their transport in the insect circulation. They are central molecular mediators of lipid mobilization and distribution.

A specific hemolymph lipoprotein class, identified as high density lipoprotein, that is necessary for diglyceride transport from the fat body cell into the hemolymph and also participates in cholesterol transport from the gut. It appears to be the major neutral lipid and sterol transport agent in the insects studied.
A hemolymph lipoprotein class identified as very high density lipoprotein. It may provide protein and lipid to the insect ovary during oogenesis.
The density class designation associated with lipoprotein I. It characterizes the transport particle involved in neutral lipid and sterol carriage in insect hemolymph.
The density class designation associated with lipoprotein II. It characterizes a hemolymph lipoprotein implicated in nutrient delivery to the ovary.
The digestive tissue from which cholesterol is transported into the hemolymph. It serves as the source setting for sterol uptake into the circulating transport system.
The reproductive tissue receiving protein and lipid during oogenesis. It is a target tissue for hemolymph lipoprotein-mediated nutrient delivery.
The process of egg development in insects. The abstract notes that lipoprotein II may support this process by delivering protein and lipid to the ovary.
A polyhydroxy steroidal insect molting hormone that is probably carried free in the hemolymph. It is part of the hormonal transport context described in the paper.

A major insect growth hormone transported by hemolymph lipoproteins in silkmoths and locusts and by a lower molecular weight hemolymph protein in the tobacco hornworm. It is a key signaling molecule in insect development.
Lipoprotein carriers present in hemolymph that transport juvenile hormone in some insect species. They represent a broader carrier class involved in hormone transport.
A hemolymph protein carrier that transports juvenile hormone in the tobacco hornworm. It represents an alternative transport mechanism to lipoprotein-mediated carriage.
An insect group specifically mentioned as a studied species in which diglycerides are abundant in hemolymph and juvenile hormone is transported by hemolymph lipoproteins.
An insect group specifically mentioned as a studied species in which diglycerides are abundant in hemolymph and juvenile hormone is transported by hemolymph lipoproteins.
An insect group cited as one of the species in which diglycerides constitute a major hemolymph neutral lipid fraction.
An insect group cited among the species in which diglycerides constitute a major hemolymph neutral lipid fraction.
An insect species specifically mentioned as using a lower molecular weight hemolymph protein to transport juvenile hormone.
The insect model organism discussed in the paper. It is the biological subject in which ecdysone-mediated developmental cell death is examined, especially during metamorphosis and tissue remodeling.

A steroid hormone that functions as the central developmental regulator in Drosophila. In this context it drives metamorphic transitions and controls programmed cell death through temporal pulses and regulation of downstream transcriptional programs.
A developmental transition in Drosophila from embryonic to larval stage. It is one of the major stage changes regulated by ecdysone signaling.
A developmental transition in Drosophila from larval to pupal stage. This metamorphic transition is tightly controlled by ecdysone and is associated with extensive programmed cell death.
The metamorphic developmental phase in which larval tissues are remodeled for pupation. It is the key biological context in which extensive programmed cell death occurs.
A regulated cell elimination process occurring during Drosophila development. It removes obsolete larval tissues and is spatially and temporally controlled by ecdysone signaling.
The larval tissue structures in Drosophila that are eliminated or remodeled during metamorphosis. They are the cellular targets of developmental programmed cell death.
Temporal bursts of the steroid hormone ecdysone during development. These pulses provide the timing signal that controls transcriptional responses and programmed cell death during metamorphosis.
Transcriptional regulators induced or controlled by ecdysone pulses. They mediate downstream gene expression programs that execute developmental cell death.

entity_name: KEY GENES INVOLVED IN CELL DEATH
description: Genes whose expression is driven by ecdysone-regulated transcription factors and that participate in the execution of programmed cell death.
The broader biological process of cellular elimination discussed in the review. It is controlled by ecdysone in specific larval and adult tissues and is central to metamorphic remodeling.
Tissue subsets in larval and adult Drosophila in which ecdysone regulates cell death. These tissues represent spatially restricted targets of developmental signaling.

A steroid hormone signal discussed as the primary developmental regulator in insect molting and metamorphosis. It binds the ecdysone receptor complex to trigger transcriptional cascades that drive stage transitions in epidermal and nervous tissues.

An insect hormone that maintains larval developmental status and modulates the outcome of ecdysteroid-driven molts. Its presence ensures larval-to-larval molting, and its absence permits metamorphic progression.

A steroid hormone receptor that binds ecdysteroids and participates in activating regulatory genes during insect molting and metamorphosis. The text notes a new isoform appearing during metamorphosis and links EcR abundance in neurons to cell fate.

A receptor partner and member of the steroid hormone receptor superfamily that complexes with EcR to mediate ecdysteroid signaling. It functions as part of the transcriptional activation machinery controlling developmental gene expression.

A 29-kDa nuclear protein in larval tissues that specifically binds juvenile hormone with high affinity. It is described as an intranuclear hormone receptor with discrete subnuclear localization and no known DNA-binding domains.

Genes directly activated by ecdysteroid signaling through EcR and ultraspiracle, producing downstream factors that repress existing gene expression and stimulate stage-specific developmental programs.
The pre-existing transcriptional program that is repressed during ecdysteroid-induced molting to allow transition to a new developmental stage.
The developmental program induced by ecdysteroid-regulated gene cascades that generates the next insect stage during molting and metamorphosis.
The developmental process by which insect larvae shed the cuticle and transition to another larval or pupal stage under hormonal control.
The developmental transition from larval to pupal/adult forms in insects, regulated by the balance of ecdysteroid and juvenile hormone signaling.
An insect tissue explicitly mentioned as one of the target tissues undergoing metamorphic regulation in the review.
An insect tissue system discussed as a site where hormone receptor signaling regulates metamorphic development and neuronal cell fate.
An insect model organism used as an example to illustrate hormone receptor control of larval molting and metamorphosis.
A model insect species used as an example in the review for studying ecdysteroid and juvenile hormone receptor-mediated developmental regulation.
A hormonal context characterized by low ecdysteroid levels that precedes appearance of a new EcR isoform and ecdysteroid-induced regulatory factors during metamorphosis.
A hormonal context characterized by elevated ecdysteroid levels that activates a new regulatory cascade leading to the pupal molt.
The tissue context in which the JH receptor is found and maintained during ecdysteroid rises, serving as the site of juvenile hormone-dependent receptor synthesis.
Neuronal cells in the larval stage where the quantity of the new EcR isoform is correlated with cell fate during adult development.
The developmental outcome of larval neurons that is correlated with the abundance of a new EcR isoform during metamorphosis and adult development.
The molt that produces the pupal stage, triggered by a new ecdysteroid-driven cascade in the absence of juvenile hormone.
The later developmental phase in which metamorphosing larval neurons show EcR isoform abundance correlated with cell fate.
A metamorphosis-associated variant of the ecdysone receptor that appears in response to low ecdysteroid and is implicated in later developmental gene regulation and neuronal cell fate.
Regulatory factors that appear during metamorphosis in response to low ecdysteroid and participate in the subsequent high-ecdysteroid cascade.

A steroid hormone that initiates Drosophila metamorphosis by inducing widespread changes in gene expression and directly inducing BR-C and E74. It functions as the upstream signaling agent in the developmental regulatory cascade described in the abstract.

An ecdysone-inducible early gene complex (BR-C) encoding families of transcription factors. It is directly induced by ecdysone and participates in regulating primary- and secondary-response genes, metamorphic development, and gene transcription.

An ecdysone-inducible early gene encoding transcription factor families. It is directly induced by ecdysone and works with BR-C in regulating ecdysone response genes, developmental gene expression, and metamorphic processes.

The protein products encoded by BR-C and E74 that regulate transcription of ecdysone primary- and secondary-response genes and may directly interact to control downstream developmental gene expression.
A class of genes directly regulated by ecdysone-induced transcription factors such as BR-C and E74. They represent early transcriptional targets in the ecdysone signaling cascade.
A class of downstream genes whose transcription is regulated by BR-C and E74 after ecdysone induction. They are part of the broader developmental gene-expression program.
The developmental transition in Drosophila that is initiated by ecdysone and regulated by BR-C and E74. It is the central biological process affected in the study.
The transcriptional program altered by ecdysone pulses and regulated by BR-C and E74. It underlies the developmental changes leading to metamorphosis.
The transcription of downstream target genes regulated by the interaction of BR-C and E74. It is a specific transcriptional outcome emphasized in the title and abstract.
A metamorphic developmental process shared by BR-C and E74 function. It is one of the morphogenetic pathways affected by these transcription factors.
A developmental transition during insect metamorphosis that is shared in function by BR-C and E74. It reflects the morphogenetic role of these genes.
The activation of early-response genes during development, shared by BR-C and E74. It is part of the ecdysone-driven transcriptional response.
A gene expression product or gene class whose expression may be directly regulated by BR-C and E74. It is mentioned as a downstream target in the developmental program.
A downstream class of genes whose expression may be directly regulated by BR-C and E74 during metamorphosis. They represent later transcriptional targets in the developmental cascade.
Developmental pathways proposed to be regulated by combinations of ecdysone primary-response genes such as BR-C and E74. They provide the broader mechanistic framework for metamorphosis.

entity_name: MUTATIONS IN THE BR-C AND E74
description: Genetic alterations in BR-C and E74 that are lethal during metamorphosis and produce similar lethal phenotypes and transcriptional alterations. They provide genetic evidence for the functional importance of these genes.
Animals carrying combined representative alleles from BR-C and E74 complementation groups. They are the experimental population used to assess shared and synergistic functions of the two genes.

The biological subject group discussed in the paper. Insects are the organismal population in which developmental control of body size and wing-body scaling is analyzed, including how hormonal regulation coordinates growth, molting, and tissue differentiation.

A developmental size endpoint representing the overall size of the organism. In this text, body size is the primary phenotype controlled by growth-regulatory mechanisms and used as the reference for scaling of body parts such as wings.
The proportional relationship between wing size and body size. It is a developmental outcome adjusted during insect growth, with wing size coordinated to body size through hormonal regulation.

The biological process of organismal and tissue enlargement discussed as being hormonally regulated. Growth is controlled by insulin and ecdysone and is terminated when the species-specific size threshold is reached.

A hormone that acts as a growth-regulatory agent in insects. In the abstract, insulin works synergistically with ecdysone to control cell growth and cell division, thereby contributing to overall body size regulation.

A hormone central to insect developmental transitions and growth control. At low concentration it supports growth, while at high levels it triggers molting and tissue differentiation; its pulse initiates the metamorphic molt and helps determine body size and wing-body scaling.
The process of cellular enlargement regulated by hormonal signaling. In this text, cell growth is one of the processes jointly controlled by insulin and ecdysone during insect development.
The process of cellular proliferation regulated during insect growth. It is controlled synergistically by insulin and ecdysone and contributes to body size determination.
A developmental process involving shedding of the exoskeleton and transition to the next stage. In the abstract, high ecdysone levels and the ecdysone pulse initiate the metamorphic molt.
The process by which tissues acquire specialized structure and function. The text states that high levels of ecdysone cause tissue differentiation during insect development.
The molt associated with metamorphic transition in insects. It is initiated by the pulse of ecdysone and marks the developmental shift after growth cessation.
Sensory structures that detect body size or stretch-related cues. In some species, they are proposed as one mechanism for sensing body size and triggering increased ecdysone secretion.

A physiological constraint used as a body-size sensing mechanism in some insect species. It is described as an alternative cue that can stimulate high-level ecdysone secretion when body size is being assessed.
An elevated hormonal secretion state that functions as a developmental trigger. It is stimulated by body-size sensing mechanisms and induces molting in the insect developmental program.
The developmental growth process of the wing. The abstract notes that wing growth occurs mostly after body growth has stopped and that wing size is adjusted through variation in ecdysone secretion.
The temporal length of ecdysone secretion, described as one factor that varies to adjust wing size relative to body size. It is part of the hormonal control of developmental scaling.
The magnitude or concentration of ecdysone secretion, described as another factor that varies to adjust wing size relative to body size. It contributes to developmental scaling control.
A population of insects undergoing complete metamorphosis; used here as the biological subject in which imaginal discs and cuticular gene regulation are discussed.

Small sac-like epithelial cell clusters in larval insects that later contribute to adult structures; they are the tissue context for the developmental and transcriptional changes described in metamorphosis.
The developmental anatomical setting in which imaginal discs form and reside during the larval stage before metamorphic transformation.
The developmental process in which insect tissues undergo major structural and functional remodeling, including cell proliferation and differentiation in imaginal discs.
Endogenous signaling agents that trigger and regulate metamorphic changes in the insect tissues discussed in the abstract.
A developmental process involving increased cell division in imaginal discs during metamorphosis.
The process by which cells acquire specialized identities during metamorphosis, contributing to tissue remodeling in imaginal discs.
The silkworm insect species used as the organismal context for the discussion of cuticular protein gene expression and hormonal responsiveness.
A gene family encoding cuticular proteins; in this text they are described by developmental expression profile and responsiveness to steroid hormones in wing discs.
A developmental stage setting in which CP genes are expressed in wing discs before pupation.
A specific imaginal disc tissue in Bombyx mori where CP genes are expressed and regulated during the prepupal stage.
A descriptive analytical framework used to classify CP genes into groups based on when they are expressed during development.
A class of hormones that modulate the responsiveness and regulation of CP gene expression during insect development.
The broader cellular remodeling events occurring during metamorphosis and regulated by hormones in insect tissues.

The broad animal population discussed as the biological subject in which developmental timing and maturation are regulated. In this context, insects undergo juvenile-to-adult transition, growth-dependent ecdysone signaling, and metamorphosis.
The developmental transition from juvenile stages to adulthood. It is the central process described, involving growth completion, hormonal control, metamorphosis, and reproductive maturation.

entity_name: GROWTH TO A SPECIES-SPECIFIC TARGET SIZE
description: A developmental growth process that reaches a species-specific threshold and acts as a trigger for downstream endocrine events. It is linked to timing of ecdysone pulses and maturation checkpoints.

A steroid hormone that functions as the key endocrine signal controlling metamorphosis and reproductive maturation in insects. Its production and release are tightly timed by developmental checkpoints and signaling circuits.
The developmental reprogramming process triggered by ecdysone pulses that drives the transition from juvenile to adult form. It is a major downstream outcome of endocrine timing control.
The developmental process by which reproductive capacity is achieved after growth completion. In the text, it is coordinated with metamorphosis and regulated by ecdysone signaling.

The integrated signaling system that monitors size-related, nutritional, and external cues to regulate the timing of ecdysone production and release. It serves as a central controller of developmental timing.
Internal signals reflecting organismal growth status and body size. These signals are monitored by the neuroendocrine system to determine when developmental progression should proceed.
Signals reflecting nutritional state that influence developmental timing. They are integrated with size-related and external cues to regulate ecdysone production and release.
Environmental signals that contribute to timing decisions in developmental progression. They modulate the neuroendocrine control of ecdysone dynamics under different environmental conditions.
Regulatory control points that govern progression to adulthood by coordinating the genetic timing program. They integrate environmental and internal signals to modulate endocrine output.
The genetically encoded developmental timing framework that enables progression to adulthood. It is regulated by checkpoints and adapted to environmental conditions.
A collection of molecular signaling routes used by developmental checkpoints to modulate ecdysone production in the prothoracic gland.
The biosynthetic process generating ecdysone. It is regulated by developmental checkpoints and signaling pathways in the prothoracic gland.
The secretion or mobilization of ecdysone into circulation. It is timed by neuroendocrine control and contributes to developmental transitions.
The endocrine tissue where signaling pathways modulate ecdysone production. It is the anatomical setting for hormone synthesis in insect developmental timing.

entity_name: AUTONOMOUS CASCADE OF FEEDFORWARD AND FEEDBACK SIGNALS
description: A self-regulating signaling cascade activated by ecdysone release that determines the duration of the hormone pulse. It includes both feedforward and feedback components.
The temporal length of each ecdysone pulse during developmental transitions. It is shaped by feedforward and feedback signaling after hormone release.
Stage-to-stage developmental changes during maturation, including transitions governed by ecdysone pulses. They are the context in which pulse duration is determined.
The model organism referenced as a conserved framework for studying developmental timing. It provides insight into the genetic mechanisms controlling juvenile-adult transition in metazoans.
The broader animal group for which conserved developmental timing mechanisms are suggested to apply. The text frames Drosophila findings as relevant to this population.

An insect steroid hormone that functions as a key signaling molecule in development and gene regulation. In this study it is the endogenous substrate whose cellular uptake is mediated by OATP transporters and whose signaling depends on EcI.
A family of membrane transport proteins implicated in the cellular import of ecdysone in insects. They are central to the paper's mechanistic focus on conserved ecdysone uptake across arthropods.

A candidate transporter protein characterized as an ecdysone importer in lepidopteran pests. It is investigated for its role in ecdysone uptake, signaling, development, and sensitivity to transporter inhibition.
A major agricultural moth pest species included as one of the lepidopteran organisms used to characterize the putative ecdysone importer. It serves as a comparative insect subject in the study.
A major agricultural moth pest species used as an in vivo and cellular study subject for EcI functional disruption and re-expression. It provides evidence for EcI's role in development and survival.
The evolutionary lineage across which OATP transporter conservation was assessed. It provides phylogenetic context for the emergence of EcI.
A broad evolutionary grouping of molting animals used as the phylogenetic scope for analyzing OATP transporter evolution. It contextualizes the inferred origin of EcI.
A lepidopteran cell line used as an experimental model to deplete and re-express EcI. It enables functional testing of EcI in ecdysone-mediated signaling and cell death.
A developmental endpoint measured after partial disruption of EcI in S. frugiperda. Decreased hatching rate indicates impaired embryonic development.
A survival endpoint in S. frugiperda that decreased following partial EcI disruption. It reflects EcI's importance for normal insect development and viability.
The organismal developmental process regulated by ecdysone signaling and dependent on EcI-mediated hormone uptake. It is implicated by reduced hatching and survival after EcI disruption.
A hormone-driven signaling process controlled by EcI in the lepidopteran cell line. It links ecdysone transport to downstream gene regulatory responses.
The downstream transcriptional control process influenced by ecdysone-mediated signaling in the cell line model. It represents a functional output of EcI-dependent hormone uptake.
A programmed cell death process induced or regulated by ecdysone signaling and shown to depend on EcI function in the cell line model.
A well-known organic anion transporter inhibitor used here as a pharmacologic agent to probe EcI sensitivity and transporter function.
The pharmacologic class of rifampicin, used to inhibit transporter activity and assess EcI-mediated ecdysone uptake and signaling.
Transporter proteins analyzed phylogenetically across Ecdysozoa to infer the evolutionary emergence of EcI. They provide the broader molecular family context for ecdysone import.

The broad biological population undergoing postembryonic development and metamorphosis described in the paper. It serves as the organismal context for the developmental and cellular remodeling processes discussed.

A subgroup of insects that undergo complete metamorphosis, characterized by extensive larval tissue destruction and adult structure formation. This population is central to the review's discussion of metamorphic remodeling.
The insect model organism emphasized as the primary system for studying metamorphosing central nervous system remodeling, ecdysone signaling, and programmed cell death.

A postembryonic developmental process in insects involving dramatic remodeling, destruction of larval structures, and generation of adult structures. It provides the overarching biological context for the CNS changes described.
The developmental period after embryogenesis during which metamorphosis occurs in insects. It frames the timing of the structural and cellular changes discussed in the abstract.

A steroid hormone that orchestrates diverse cellular events during insect metamorphosis, including remodeling and programmed cell death. It functions as a key upstream regulator in the developmental program.
The signaling pathway mediated by ecdysone that coordinates metamorphic cellular events. It is highlighted as a central regulatory mechanism in the review.

The insect CNS is the tissue system extensively remodeled during metamorphosis to support new sensory processing, locomotion, and decision-making functions. It is the main anatomical focus of the review.
Abbreviation for central nervous system, referring to the neural tissue undergoing extensive metamorphic remodeling in insects.
A regulated cell elimination process that is integral to metamorphic development. It removes obsolete larval tissues and excess cells and contributes to adult CNS formation.
Abbreviation for programmed cell death, the regulated process discussed as essential for metamorphic tissue remodeling and CNS establishment.
A subset of neuronal cells in the metamorphosing CNS that undergo programmed cell death during remodeling. Their elimination contributes to adult CNS formation.
Supportive neural cells in the CNS that are selectively eliminated by programmed cell death during metamorphosis. They are part of the cellular remodeling process.
Larval cells that persist into metamorphosis and are reshaped rather than eliminated to help establish the adult CNS. They represent a cellular substrate for remodeling.
Structures present in the larval stage that are destroyed during metamorphosis. Their removal is a hallmark of complete metamorphic remodeling.
Adult structures generated during metamorphosis to replace larval structures. They represent the developmental endpoint of remodeling.
The mature central nervous system established after metamorphic remodeling and programmed cell death. It is the functional neural architecture produced by developmental reorganization.
The sensory information that the remodeled CNS must process after metamorphosis. This reflects a functional demand driving CNS restructuring.
The altered locomotor behaviors that the remodeled CNS must coordinate in the adult insect. This is a functional outcome of CNS reorganization.
Advanced neural processing functions that the remodeled CNS must support in the adult insect. It reflects the functional significance of CNS metamorphic remodeling.
The set of molecular and cellular changes associated with programmed cell death and CNS remodeling during metamorphosis. This is a broad process category summarized in the review.

A steroid hormone that serves as the central regulatory molecular signal in insect developmental transitions. In this text, it is the key biological feature whose release, signaling, and stage- and tissue-specific responses are being reviewed.
The developmental changes in insects controlled by ecdysone, including progression through major life-history stages. It is the primary biological process discussed as being regulated by the hormone.
The fruit fly model organism used as the experimental system for studying ecdysone biology and insect metamorphosis. It provides the molecular genetic tools referenced in the abstract.

Experimental genetic and molecular approaches applied in Drosophila melanogaster to investigate ecdysone action and developmental regulation. These tools enable mechanistic study of signaling and metamorphosis.
The developmental remodeling process in insects that is studied in relation to ecdysone signaling. It represents a major downstream biological process influenced by hormonal control.
The timing and regulation of hormone release, identified as one of the major aspects of ecdysone biology discussed in the review. It is a process upstream of downstream developmental responses.

entity_name: STAGE- AND TISSUE-SPECIFIC RESPONSES TO ECDYSONE
description: Context-dependent biological responses to ecdysone that vary by developmental stage and tissue type. This process captures the specificity of hormonal action emphasized in the abstract.
Regulatory feedback mechanisms that modulate ecdysone signaling. It is highlighted as a major aspect of ecdysone biology and contributes to control of signaling dynamics.
The signaling pathway mediated by ecdysone that coordinates developmental transitions and responses. It is the central pathway whose regulation and coordination are reviewed.
The temporal regulation of when ecdysone is released, which is a key determinant of developmental progression. The abstract identifies factors controlling this timing as a major focus.

A steroid hormone discussed as a central endocrine signal in insect metamorphosis. It is part of the molecular signaling framework whose evolution and interaction with juvenile hormone are reviewed, and it contributes to regulating developmental transitions.

A key insect hormone that suppresses morphogenesis and promotes juvenile developmental states. In the text, it is described as essential for the evolution of metamorphosis, delaying imaginal growth and influencing the formation of larval and imaginal structures.

The developmental process of transformation from one insect life stage to another, especially complete metamorphosis. It is the central biological process under discussion and is linked to endocrine signaling changes involving ecdysone and juvenile hormone.

A derived developmental program in insects involving a distinct larval stage and later transformation into adult form. The review focuses on its evolution and how it has altered endocrine signaling pathways.

Hormone-mediated signaling processes that regulate insect development. The text emphasizes that metamorphosis has influenced the molecular aspects of endocrine signaling, particularly those involving ecdysone and juvenile hormone.

The process of tissue and body form development that juvenile hormone suppresses in early developmental contexts. It is functionally important for controlling whether embryos proceed toward larval differentiation.

An early developmental transition induced by juvenile hormone in the described evolutionary context. It is part of the mechanism by which transitional stages are converted into functional larval stages.

A transitional developmental stage in hemimetabolous insects referenced as a target of juvenile hormone action. It is important as the stage that must be transformed into a functional larval stage in the evolutionary scenario described.
A group of insects with incomplete metamorphosis. They are used as a comparative evolutionary population in the discussion of how juvenile hormone shapes developmental transitions.
The developmental outcome in which the organism attains a viable larval form. It is described as the result of juvenile hormone-mediated suppression and differentiation changes.
Growth associated with imaginal structures that is delayed in the ancestral condition until juvenile hormone disappears. It is a key developmental process in the emergence of adult structures.
The final larval developmental stage during which juvenile hormone disappears in the ancestral condition. It serves as a temporal context for the release of imaginal-related growth.

A derived insect group characterized by complete metamorphosis. The text uses this group to describe evolutionary changes in tissue sensitivity to juvenile hormone and the emergence of imaginal discs.
A subset of tissues in holometabolous insects that have escaped juvenile hormone suppression. These tissues are important because they can initiate early growth and form imaginal discs.
The inhibitory effect of juvenile hormone on developmental progression and tissue growth. It is a mechanistic process central to the evolutionary discussion of metamorphosis.
Developing imaginal structures that begin growth early in derived insect groups. They represent a developmental outcome of tissues escaping juvenile hormone suppression.

The molecular-level features of ecdysone-mediated signaling discussed as being influenced by the evolution of complete metamorphosis. This reflects changes in endocrine regulation across insect development.

The molecular-level features of juvenile hormone signaling that may have been altered by the evolution of complete metamorphosis. It is part of the broader endocrine evolution discussed in the review.
Early developmental subjects in basal insect groups that are acted on by juvenile hormone. They are relevant as the developmental stage where hormone-mediated suppression of morphogenesis occurs.
Evolutionarily ancestral insect lineages used for comparison in the review. They provide the context in which juvenile hormone acts on embryos to influence developmental fate.
